params.text:
AN ICE CUBE, HEATED UNTIL IT BOILS AWAY

Ice is water whose molecules have stopped tumbling past each other
and locked into a pattern. Every molecule holds on to four
neighbours, and together they make a honeycomb of six-sided rings.
Melting is that pattern breaking up. Boiling is the molecules
letting go of each other altogether.

Here you build a tiny ice cube -- 768 water molecules, 3 nanometres
across; ten million of them side by side would make one cube for a
drink -- let it float in empty space, and heat it: from colder than
any freezer to far hotter than any kettle, in one run.

Press Run. Everything takes a few minutes; read the notes while it
works. Point at any socket to see what kind of file goes through
it; Help (the ? at the top) lists them all.

1. BUILD THE CUBE

'Ice crystal' puts every molecule where ice puts it. Each oxygen
(red) points its two hydrogens (white) at two of its four
neighbours. Those hydrogen bonds are what hold ice together.

The water model is TIP4P/Ice: a water molecule drawn as four points
-- an oxygen, two hydrogens, and one invisible point that carries the
negative charge. Its numbers were chosen so that its ice melts at
the right temperature: 272 K, where real ice melts at 273 K,
0 degrees C.

'Define box' puts the cube in the middle of a 5.5 nm box of empty
space. Simulation boxes repeat in every direction, so the box has to
be big enough that the cube never feels the copy of itself next door.

The second row lets the cube settle: every molecule is nudged into
place before the clock starts. No time passes in this step.

params.raw:
; Minimisation: let every molecule settle into place.
;
; A crystal built from a recipe is never quite right -- a hydrogen a little
; too close to a neighbour here, a molecule a little twisted there. This walks
; every molecule downhill in energy until nothing is pushing hard any more.
; No time passes, and nothing moves afterwards: the cube is standing
; perfectly still, which is what 0 K, absolute zero, means.
integrator      = steep
emtol           = 100       ; stop when no force is bigger than this
nsteps          = 5000      ; or after this many tries

cutoff-scheme   = Verlet
coulombtype     = PME       ; every charge feels every other charge
rcoulomb        = 1.0       ; nm
vdwtype         = cut-off   ; molecules further apart than rvdw ignore each other's size
rvdw            = 1.0       ; nm
pbc             = xyz       ; the box repeats in every direction

params.text:
2. HEAT IT: 200 K TO 1000 K

Every molecule is given a speed that matches 200 K, minus 73
degrees C, and a thermostat keeps the temperature where it is told.
Then it is told to climb: slowly to 400 K over the first 100
picoseconds, then fast to 1000 K over the next 100. That is 100,000
steps of 2 femtoseconds each; a femtosecond is a millionth of a
billionth of a second.

What happens, in order:
- ice for about the first 30 ps: the molecules shiver harder and
  harder, but the honeycomb holds;
- then it melts, from the surface inwards, and by about 70 ps, near
  340 K, it has pulled itself into a round drop;
- a drop of hot water for about 40 ps, far above 100 degrees C;
- then it boils away: molecules fly off, a few at first, then in a
  rush;
- gas for the last 30 or 40 ps: the molecules fill the whole box.

Real ice melts at 273 K and real water boils at 373 K. Here both
happen later, because everything has to happen within 200
picoseconds: the heat arrives faster than a crystal can come apart,
and at 373 K a molecule escapes from the drop only now and then.

params.raw:
; The ice cube heated in one run, from 200 K to 1000 K.
;
; 200 K is minus 73 degrees C, colder than any freezer. 1000 K is over 700
; degrees C. The thermostat's target climbs as the run goes: slowly to 400 K
; over the first 100 ps, so the ice has time to melt and the drop time to
; settle, then fast to 1000 K over the next 100 ps, where the drop boils away.
; To heat it differently, change the numbers on the annealing lines, and
; nsteps to match the last time on them.
integrator           = md
dt                   = 0.002     ; one step is 2 femtoseconds (0.002 ps)
nsteps               = 100000    ; 100,000 steps: 200 picoseconds

nstxout-compressed   = 250       ; save a picture every 250 steps (0.5 ps)
nstenergy            = 500       ; and the energies, every 1 ps
nstlog               = 5000

cutoff-scheme        = Verlet
coulombtype          = PME
rcoulomb             = 1.0
vdwtype              = cut-off
rvdw                 = 1.0
pbc                  = xyz

; The thermostat: it keeps the temperature at its target, by speeding the
; molecules up or slowing them down a little at every step.
tcoupl               = v-rescale
tc-grps              = System
tau_t                = 0.1       ; how quickly it corrects, in ps
ref_t                = 200       ; the target at the start

; Annealing: the target moves, in straight lines between these points.
; 200 K at 0 ps, 400 K at 100 ps, 1000 K at 200 ps.
annealing            = single
annealing-npoints    = 3
annealing-time       = 0 100 200
annealing-temp       = 200 400 1000

; Give every molecule a speed to start with, picked at random the way
; speeds are spread at 200 K.
gen_vel              = yes
gen_temp             = 200
gen_seed             = 2026

; No pressure control: around the cube there is nothing but empty space, and
; that is where the gas goes.
pcoupl               = no

; Take away any drift of the whole lot, so it does not wander off. Only the
; drift: molecules that boil off fly out through one side of the box and come
; back in through the opposite one, since the box repeats in every direction,
; and stopping any spin as well goes wrong once they do.
comm-mode            = linear

params.measure: Radius of gyration: how spread out it is (gyrate)

params.text:
3. WHAT THE PICTURES SAY

TEMPERATURE: the thermometer. It follows the thermostat: a gentle
slope for 100 ps, then a steep one. Use it to read off how hot it
was at any moment in the other graphs.

COUNT THE ICE: how many molecules still sit in the honeycomb, frame
by frame. It starts well below 768, because a molecule on the
surface has too few neighbours to pass the test, and drops within
the first picosecond: once the molecules shiver, some fail the
strict test even though the crystal is still there. Its fall to
zero is the melting.

SIZE: the radius of gyration, roughly how far the molecules are from
the middle, on average. It shrinks a little as the cube melts: a
ball is more compact than a cube, and liquid water packs its
molecules closer together than ice does, which is why ice floats.
Then it shoots up as the drop boils away, and levels off once the
gas fills the box evenly.

ENERGY: how tightly the molecules hold on to each other, the
potential energy. The more negative, the tighter. It climbs the whole
way, because the heat goes into pulling the molecules apart; fastest
while the drop boils away, and hardly at all once it is all gas,
when the molecules have almost nothing left to let go of.

THE MOVIE: one dot per molecule, its oxygen. Press play; drag to
turn it.
